entries.bc80afb70dec5aa1be34c6f0411a9b148e4428c7: <div sID="gen20193" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Amos.7" sID="Amos.7"/> <div eID="gen20193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20194" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20195" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. God contending with Israel, by the judgments, but are reprieved, and the judgments turned away at the prayer of Amos, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.1-Amos.7.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. 2. God's patience is at length worn out by their obstinacy, and they are rejected, and sentenced to utter ruin, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.7-Amos.7.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. II. Israel contending with God, by the opposition given to his prophet. 1. Amaziah informs against Amos (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.10-Amos.7.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>) and does what he can to rid the country of him as a public nuisance, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.12-Amos.7.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>. 2. Amos justifies himself in what he did as a prophet (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.14-Amos.7.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>) and denounces the judgments of God against Amaziah his prosecutor (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.16-Amos.7.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>); for, when the contest is between God and man, it is easy to foresee, it is very easy to foretel, who will come off with the worst of it.
entries.2244a6bc7993893ae964e6760e51b8c8c2d99075: <div eID="gen20195" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20194" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Intercession for Israel; Ruin of Israel Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 785.)</title> <div sID="gen20196" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus hath the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> shewed unto me; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and, lo, <hi type="italic">it was</hi> the latter growth after the king's mowings. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it came to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, O Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> small. <hi type="super">3</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> repented for this: It shall not be, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">4</hi> Thus hath the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> shewed unto me: and, behold, the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> called to contend by fire, and it devoured the great deep, and did eat up a part. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then said I, O Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , cease, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> small. <hi type="super">6</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> repented for this: This also shall not be, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> Thus he shewed me: and, behold, the Lord stood upon a wall <hi type="italic">made</hi> by a plumb-line, with a plumb-line in his hand. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Amos, what seest thou? And I said, A plumb-line. Then said the Lord, Behold, I will set a plumb-line in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more: <hi type="super">9</hi> And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. <div eID="gen20196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20197" type="x-p"/> We here see that God bears long, but that he will not bear always, with a provoking people, both these God here showed the prophet: <hi type="italic">Thus hath the Lord God showed me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.7.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.4">4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.7">7</reference>. He showed him what was present, foreshowed him what was to come, gave him the knowledge both of what he did and of what he designed; for the <hi type="italic">Lord God reveals his secret unto his servants the prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">ch. iii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen20197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20198" type="x-p"/> I. We have here two instances of God's sparing mercy, remembered in the midst of judgment, the narratives of which are so much like one another that they will be best considered together, and very considerable they are. <div eID="gen20198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20199" type="x-p"/> 1. God is here coming forth against this sinful nation, first by one judgment and then by another. (1.) He begins with the judgment of famine. The prophet saw this in vision. He saw God <hi type="italic">forming grasshoppers,</hi> or <hi type="italic">locusts,</hi> and bringing them up upon the land, to eat up the fruits of it, and so to strip it of its beauty and starve its inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.1">v. 1</reference>. God formed these grasshoppers, not only as they were his creatures (and much of the wisdom and power of God appears in the formation of minute animals, as much in the structure of an ant as of an elephant), but as they were instruments of his wrath. God is said to <hi type="italic">frame evil</hi> against a sinful people, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jer. xviii. 11</reference>. These grasshoppers were framed on purpose to <hi type="italic">eat up the grass of the land;</hi> and vast numbers of them were prepared accordingly. They were sent <hi type="italic">in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth, after the king's mowings.</hi> See here how the judgment was mitigated by the mercy that went before it. God could have sent these insects to eat up the grass at the beginning of the first growth, in the spring, when the grass was most needed, was most plentiful, and was the best in its kind; but God suffered that to grow, and suffered them to gather it in; the king's mowings were safely housed, for <hi type="italic">the king himself is served from the field</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.9">Eccl. v. 9</reference>), and could as ill be without his mowings as without any other branch of his revenues. Uzziah, who was now king of Judah, <hi type="italic">loved husbandry,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.10">2 Chron. xxvi. 10</reference>. But the grasshoppers were commissioned to eat up only the <hi type="italic">latter growth</hi> (the edgrew we call it in the country), the after-grass, which is of little value in comparison with the former. The mercies which God give us, and continues to us, are more numerous and more valuable than those he removes from us, which is a good reason why we should be thankful and not complain. The remembrance of the mercies of the former growth should make us submissive to the will of God when we meet with disappointments in the latter growth. The prophet, in vision, saw this judgment prevailing far. These grasshoppers <hi type="italic">ate up the grass of the land,</hi> which should have been for the cattle, which the owners must of course suffer by. Some understand this figuratively of a wasting destroying army brought upon them. In the days of Jeroboam the kingdom of Israel began to recover itself from the desolations it had been under in the former reigns (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2 Kings xiv. 25</reference>); the latter growth shot up, after the mowings of the kings of Syria, which we read of <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.3">2 Kings xiii. 3</reference>. And then God commissioned the king of Assyria with an army of caterpillars to come upon them and lay them waste, that nation spoken of <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">ch. vi. 14</reference>, which afflicted them <hi type="italic">from the entering of Hamath to the river of the wilderness,</hi> which seems to refer to <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2 Kings xiv. 25</reference>, where Jeroboam is said to have restored their coast <hi type="italic">from the entering of Hamath to the sea of the plain.</hi> God can bring all to ruin when we think all is in some good measure repaired. (2.) He proceeds to the judgment of fire, to show that he has many arrows in his quiver, many ways of humbling a sinful nation (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord God called to contend by fire.</hi> He contended, for God's judgment upon a people are his controversies with them; in them he prosecutes his action against them; and his controversies are neither causeless nor groundless. He <hi type="italic">called to contend;</hi> he did by his prophets give them notice of his controversy, and drew up a declaration, setting forth the meaning of it. Or he called for his angels, or other ministers of his justice, that were to be employed in it. A fire was kindled among them, by which perhaps is meant a great drought (the heat of the sun, which should have warmed the earth, scorched it, and burnt up the roots of the grass which the locusts had eaten the spires of), or a raging fever, which was as a fire in their bones, which devoured and ate up multitudes, or lightning, fire from heaven, which consumed their houses, as Sodom and Gomorrah were consumed (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.11">ch. iv. 11</reference>), or it was the burning of their cities, either by accident or by the hand of the enemy, for fire and sword used to go together; thus were the towns wasted, as the country was by the grasshoppers. This fire, which God called for, did terrible execution; it <hi type="italic">devoured the great deep,</hi> as the fire that fell from heaven on Elijah's altar licked up the water that was in the trench. Though the water designed for the stopping and quenching of this fire was as the water of the great deep, yet it devoured it; for who, or what, can stand before a fire kindled by the wrath of God! It did <hi type="italic">eat up a part,</hi> a great part, of the cities where it was sent; or it was as the fire at Taberah, which <hi type="italic">consumed the outermost parts of the camp</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.1">Num. xi. 1</reference>); when some were overthrown others were <hi type="italic">as brands plucked out of the fire.</hi> All deserved to be devoured, but it ate up only a part, for God does not stir up all his wrath. <div eID="gen20199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20200" type="x-p"/> 2. The prophet goes forth to meet him in the way of his judgments, and by prayer seeks to turn away his wrath, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.2">v. 2</reference>. When he saw, in vision, what dreadful work these caterpillars made, that they had eaten up in a manner <hi type="italic">all the grass of the land</hi> (he foresaw they would do so, if suffered to go on), then he said, <hi type="italic">O Lord God! forgive, I beseech thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.2">v. 2</reference>); <hi type="italic">cease, I beseech thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.7.5">v. 5</reference>. He that foretold the judgment in his preaching to the people, yet deprecated it in his intercessions for them. <hi type="italic">He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee.</hi> It was the business of prophets to pray for those to whom they prophesied, and so to make it appear that though they denounced they did not <hi type="italic">desire the woeful day. Therefore,</hi> God showed his prophets the evils coming, that they might befriend the people, not only by warning them, but by praying for them, and <hi type="italic">standing in the gap,</hi> to turn away God's wrath, as Moses, that great prophet, often did. Now observe here, <div eID="gen20200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20201" type="x-p"/> (1.) The prophet's prayer: <hi type="italic">O Lord God!</hi> [1.] <hi type="italic">Forgive, I beseech thee,</hi> and take away the sin, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.2">v. 2</reference>. He sees sin at the bottom of the trouble, and therefore concludes that the pardon of sin must be at the bottom of deliverance, and prays for that in the first place. Note, Whatever calamity we are under, personal or public, the forgiveness of sin is that which we should be most earnest with God for. [2.] <hi type="italic">Cease, I beseech thee,</hi> and take away the judgment; cease the fire, cease the controversy; <hi type="italic">cause they anger towards us to cease.</hi> This follows upon the forgiveness of sin. Take away the cause and effect will cease. Note, Those whom God contends with will soon find what need they have to cry for a cessation of arms; and there are hopes that though God has begun, and proceeded far, in his controversy, yet it may be obtained. <div eID="gen20201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20202" type="x-p"/> (2.) The prophet's plea to enforce this prayer: <hi type="italic">By whom shall Jacob arise, for he is small?</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.7.2">v. 2</reference>. And it is repeated (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.5">v. 5</reference>) and yet no vain repetition. Christ, <hi type="italic">in his agony,</hi> prayed earnestly, <hi type="italic">saying the same words,</hi> again and again. [1.] It is Jacob that he is interceding for, the professing people of God, called by his name, calling on his name, the seed of Jacob, his chosen, and in covenant with him. It it Jacob's case that is in this prayer spread before the God of Jacob. [2.] <hi type="italic">Jacob is small,</hi> very small already, weakened and brought low by former judgments; and therefore, if these come, he will be quite ruined and brought to nothing. The people are few; <hi type="italic">the dust of Jacob,</hi> which was once innumerable, is now soon counted. Those few are feeble (it is <hi type="italic">the worm Jacob,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.41.14">Isa. xli. 14</reference>); they are unable to help themselves or one another. Sin will soon make a great people small, will diminish the numerous, impoverish the plenteous, and weaken the courageous. [3.] <hi type="italic">By whom shall he arise?</hi> He has fallen, and cannot help himself up, and he has no friend to help him, none to raise him, unless the hand of God do it; what will become of him, then, if the hand that should raise him to stretched out against him? Note, When the state of God's church is very low and very helpless it is proper to be recommended by our prayers to God's pity. <div eID="gen20202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20203" type="x-p"/> 3. God graciously lets fall his controversy, in answer to the prophet's prayer, once and again (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord repented for this.</hi> He did not change his mind, for he is one mind and who can turn him? But he changed his way, took another course, and determined to deal in mercy and not in wrath. He said, <hi type="italic">It shall not be.</hi> And again (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">This also shall not be.</hi> The caterpillars were countermanded, were remanded; a stop was put to the progress of the fire, and thus a reprieve was granted. See the power of prayer, of <hi type="italic">effectual fervent</hi> prayer, and how much it <hi type="italic">avails,</hi> what great things it prevails for. A stop has many a time been put to a judgment by making <hi type="italic">supplication to the Judge.</hi> This was not the first time that Israel's life was begged, and so saved. See what a blessing praying people, praying prophets, are to a land, and therefore how highly they ought to be valued. Ruin would many a time have broken in if they had not stood in the breach, and made good the pass. See how ready, how swift, God is to show mercy, how he <hi type="italic">waits to be gracious.</hi> Amos moves for a reprieve, and obtains it, because God inclines to grant it and looks about to see if there be any that will intercede for it, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Isa. lix. 16</reference>. Nor are former reprieves objected against further instances of mercy, but are rather encouragements to pray and hope for them. This also shall not be, any more than that. It is the glory of God that he <hi type="italic">multiplies to pardon,</hi> that he spares, and forgives, to more than seventy times seven times. <div eID="gen20203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20204" type="x-p"/> II. We have here the rejection of those at last who had been often reprieved and yet never reclaimed, reduced to straits and yet never reduced to their God and their duty. This is represented to the prophet by a vision (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.7-Amos.7.8">v. 7, 8</reference>) and an express prediction of utter ruin, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.9">v. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen20204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20205" type="x-p"/> 1. The vision is of a <hi type="italic">plumb-line,</hi> a line with a plummet at the end of it, such as masons and bricklayers use to run up a wall by, that they may work it straight and true, and by rule. (1.) Israel was a wall, a strong wall, which God himself had reared, as a bulwark, or wall of defence, to his sanctuary, which he set up among them. The Jewish church says of herself (<reference osisRef="Song.8.10">Cant. viii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers.</hi> This wall was <hi type="italic">made by a plumb-line,</hi> very exact and firm. So happy was its constitution, so well compacted, and every thing so well ordered according to the model; it had long stood fast as a wall of brass. But, (2.) God now <hi type="italic">stands upon</hi> this wall, not to hold it up, but to tread it down, or, rather, to consider what he should do with it. He <hi type="italic">stands upon it with a plumb-line in his hand,</hi> to take measure of it, that it may appear to be a bowing, bulging wall. <hi type="italic">Recti est index sui et oblique—This plumb-line would discover where it was crooked.</hi> Thus God would bring the people of Israel to the trial, would discover their wickedness, and show wherein they erred; and he would likewise bring his judgments upon them according to equity, would set a <hi type="italic">plumb-line in the midst of them,</hi> to mark how far their wall must be pulled down, as David measured the <hi type="italic">Moabites with a line</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2 Sam. viii. 2</reference>) to <hi type="italic">put them to death.</hi> And, when God is coming to the ruin of a people, he is said to <hi type="italic">lay judgment to the line and righteousness to the plummet;</hi> for when he punishes it is with exactness. It is now determined: "<hi type="italic">I will not again pass by them any more;</hi> they shall not be spared and reprieved as they have been; their punishment shall not be <hi type="italic">turned away,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3">ch. i. 3</reference>. Note, God's patience, which has long been sinned against, will at length be sinned away; and the time will come when those that have been spared often shall be no longer spared. <hi type="italic">My spirit shall not always strive.</hi> After frequent reprieves, yet a day of execution will come. <div eID="gen20205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20206" type="x-p"/> 2. The prediction is of utter ruin, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.9">v. 9</reference>. (1.) The body of the people shall be destroyed, with all those things that were their ornament and defence. They are here called <hi type="italic">Isaac</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">Israel, the house of Isaac</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.16">v. 16</reference>), some think in allusion to the signification of Isaac's name; it is <hi type="italic">laughter;</hi> they shall become a jest among all their neighbours; their neighbours shall <hi type="italic">laugh at them.</hi> The desolation shall fasten upon their high places and their <hi type="italic">sanctuaries,</hi> either their <hi type="italic">castles</hi> or their <hi type="italic">temples,</hi> both built on high places. Their castles they thought safe, and their temples sacred as sanctuaries. These shall be <hi type="italic">laid waste,</hi> to punish them for their idolatry and to make them ashamed of their carnal confidences, which were the two things for which God had a controversy with them. When these were made desolate they might read their sin and folly in their punishment. (2.) The royal family shall sink first, as an earnest of the ruin of the whole kingdom: <hi type="italic">I will rise against the house of Jeroboam,</hi> Jeroboam the second, who was now king of the ten tribes; his family was extirpated in his son Zecharias, who was <hi type="italic">slain with the sword before the people,</hi> by Shallum who <hi type="italic">conspired against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.10">2 Kings xv. 10</reference>. How unrighteous soever the instruments were, God was righteous, and in them God rose up against that idolatrous family. Even king's houses will be no shelter against the sword of God's wrath.
entries.40b2738ebaaf5f273f6179b4507fb5256383ebca: <div eID="gen20206" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Amaziah's Charge against Amos; Amaziah's Doom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 785.)</title> <div sID="gen20207" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. <hi type="super">11</hi> For thus Amos saith, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land. <hi type="super">12</hi> Also Amaziah said unto Amos, O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: <hi type="super">13</hi> But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king's chapel, and it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king's court. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I <hi type="italic">was</hi> no prophet, neither <hi type="italic">was</hi> I a prophet's son; but I <hi type="italic">was</hi> a herdman, and a gatherer of sycamore fruit: <hi type="super">15</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> took me as I followed the flock, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. <hi type="super">16</hi> Now therefore hear thou the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : Thou sayest, Prophesy not against Israel, and drop not <hi type="italic">thy word</hi> against the house of Isaac. <hi type="super">17</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Thy wife shall be a harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword, and thy land shall be divided by line; and thou shalt die in a polluted land: and Israel shall surely go into captivity forth of his land. <div eID="gen20207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20208" type="x-p"/> One would have expected, 1. That what we met with in the former part of the chapter would awaken the people to repentance, when they saw that they were reprieved in order that they might have <hi type="italic">space to repent</hi> and that they could not obtain a pardon unless they did repent. 2. That it would endear the prophet Amos to them, who had not only shown his good-will to them in praying against the judgments that invaded them, but had prevailed to turn away those judgments, which, if they had had any sense of gratitude, would have gained him an interest in their affections. But it fell out quite contrary; they continue impenitent, and the next news we hear of Amos is that he is persecuted. Note, As it is the praise of great saints that they pray for those that are enemies to them, so it is the shame of many great sinners that they are enemies to those who pray for them, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Ps. xxxv. 13, 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">cix. 4</reference>. We have here, <div eID="gen20208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20209" type="x-p"/> I. The malicious information brought to the king against the prophet Amos, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.10-Amos.7.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. The informer was <hi type="italic">Amaziah the priest of Bethel,</hi> the chief of the priests that ministered to the golden calf there, the <hi type="italic">president of Bethel</hi> (so some read it), that had the principal hand in civil affairs there. He complained against Amos, not only because he prophesied without license from him, but because he prophesied against his altars, which would soon be deserted and demolished if Amos's preaching could but gain credit. Thus the shrine-makers at Ephesus hated Paul, because his preaching tended to spoil their trade. Note, Great pretenders to sanctity are commonly the worst enemies to those who are really sanctified. Priests have been the most bitter persecutors. Amaziah brings an information to Jeroboam against Amos. Observe, 1. The crime he is charged with is no less than treason: "<hi type="italic">Amos has conspired against thee,</hi> to depose and murder thee; he aims at succeeding thee, and therefore is taking the most effectual way to weaken thee. He sows the seeds of sedition in the hearts of the good subjects of the king, and makes them disaffected to him and his government, that he may draw them by degrees from their allegiance; upon this account <hi type="italic">the land is not able to bear his words.</hi>" It is slyly insinuated to the king that the country was exasperated against him, and it is given in as their sense that his preaching was intolerable, and such as nobody could be reconciled to, such as the times would by no means bear, that is, the men of the times would not. Both the impudence of his supposed treason, and the bad influence it would have upon the country, are intimated in that part of the charge, that he conspired against the king in the midst of the house of Israel. Note, It is no new thing for the accusers of the brethren to misrepresent them as enemies to the king and kingdom, as traitors to their prince and troublers of the land, when really they are the best friends to both. And it is common for designing men to assert that as the sense of the country which is far from being so. And yet here, I doubt, it was too true, that the people could not bear plain dealing any more than the priests. 2. The words laid in the indictment for the support of this charge (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Amos says</hi> (and they have witnesses ready to prove it) <hi type="italic">Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall be led away captive;</hi> and hence they infer that he is an enemy to his king and country, and not to be tolerated. See the malice of Amaziah; he does not tell the king how Amos had interceded for Israel, and by his intercession had turned away first one judgment and then another, and did not let fall his intercession till he saw the decree had gone forth; he does not tell him that these threatenings were conditional, and that he had often assured them that if they would repent and reform the ruin should be prevented. Nay, it was not true that he said, <hi type="italic">Jeroboam shall die by the sword,</hi> nor did he so die (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.28">2 Kings xiv. 28</reference>), but that God would <hi type="italic">rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.7.9">v. 9</reference>. God's prophets and ministers have often had occasion to make David's complaint (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.5">Ps. lvi. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Every day they wrest my words.</hi> But shall it be made the watchman's crime, when he sees the sword coming, to give warning to the people, that they may get themselves secured? or the physician's crime to tell his patient of the danger of his disease, that he may use means for the cure of it? What enemies are foolish men to themselves, to their own peace, to their best friends! It does not appear that Jeroboam took any notice of this information; perhaps he reverenced a prophet, and stood more in awe of the divine authority than Amaziah his priest did. <div eID="gen20209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20210" type="x-p"/> II. The method he used to persuade Amos to withdraw and quit the country (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.12-Amos.7.13">v. 12, 13</reference>); when he could not gain his point with the king to have Amos imprisoned, banished, or put to death, or at least to have him frightened into silence or flight, he tried what he could do by fair means to get rid of him; he insinuated himself into his acquaintance, and with all the arts of wheedling endeavored to persuade him to go and prophesy in the <hi type="italic">land of Judah,</hi> and not at Bethel. He owns him to be a seer, and does not pretend to enjoin him silence, but suggests to him, <div eID="gen20210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20211" type="x-p"/> 1. That Bethel was not a proper place for him to exercise his ministry in, for it was <hi type="italic">the king's chapel,</hi> or <hi type="italic">sanctuary,</hi> where he had his idols and their altars and priests; and it was <hi type="italic">the king's court,</hi> or <hi type="italic">the house of the kingdom,</hi> where the royal family resided and where were set the thrones of judgment; and therefore <hi type="italic">prophesy not any more</hi> here. And why not? (1.) Because Amos is too plain and blunt a preacher for the court and the king's chapel. Those that <hi type="italic">wear silk and fine clothing,</hi> and speak silken soft words, are fit for king's palaces. (2.) Because the worship that is in the king's chapel will be a continual vexation and trouble to Amos; let him therefore get far enough from it, and what the eye sees not the heart grieves not for. (3.) Because it was not fit that the king and his house should be affronted in their own court and chapel by the reproofs and threatenings which Amos was continually teazing them with in the name of the Lord; as if it were the prerogative of the prince, and the privilege of the peers, when they are running headlong upon a precipice, not to be told of their danger. (4.) Because he could not expect any countenance or encouragement there, but, on the contrary, to be bantered and ridiculed by some and to be threatened and brow-beaten by others; however, he could not think to make any converts there, or to persuade any from that idolatry which was supported by the authority and example of the king. To preach his doctrine there was but (as we say) to run his head against a post; and therefore <hi type="italic">prophesy no more</hi> there. But, <div eID="gen20211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20212" type="x-p"/> 2. He persuades him that the land of Judah was the fittest place for him to set up in: <hi type="italic">Flee thee away</hi> thither with all speed, and <hi type="italic">there eat bread,</hi> and <hi type="italic">prophesy there.</hi> There thou wilt be safe; there thou wilt be welcome; the king's court and chapel there are on thy side; the prophets there will second thee; the priests and princes there will take notice of thee, and allow thee an honourable maintenance. See here, (1.) How willing wicked men are to get clear of their faithful reprovers, and how ready to <hi type="italic">say to the seers, See not,</hi> or See not for us; the two witnesses were a torment to those that dwelt on the earth (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.10">Rev. xi. 10</reference>), and it were indeed a pity that men should be <hi type="italic">tormented before the time,</hi> but that it is in order to the preventing of eternal torment. (2.) How apt worldly men are to measure others by themselves. Amaziah, as a priest, aimed at nothing but the profits of his place, and he thought Amos, as a prophet, had the same views, and therefore advised him to prophesy were he might <hi type="italic">eat bread,</hi> where he might be sure to have as much as he chose; whereas Amos was to prophesy where God appointed him, and where there was most need of him, not where he would get most money. Note, Those that make gain their godliness, and are governed by the hopes of wealth and preferment themselves, are ready to think these the most powerful inducements with others also. <div eID="gen20212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20213" type="x-p"/> III. The reply which Amos made to these suggestions of Amaziah's. He did not <hi type="italic">consult with flesh and blood,</hi> nor was it his care to enrich himself, but to <hi type="italic">make full proof of his ministry,</hi> and to be found faithful in the discharge of it, not to sleep in a whole skin, but to keep a good conscience; and therefore he resolved to abide by his post, and, in answer to Amaziah, <div eID="gen20213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20214" type="x-p"/> 1. He justified himself in his constant adherence to his work and to his place (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.14-Amos.7.15">v. 14, 15</reference>); and that which he was sure would not only bear him out, but bind him to it, was that he had a divine warrant and commission for it: "<hi type="italic">I was no prophet, nor prophet's son,</hi> neither born nor bred to the office, not originally designed for a prophet, as Samuel and Jeremiah, not educated in the schools of the prophets, as many others were; but <hi type="italic">I was a herdsman,</hi> a keeper of cattle, and <hi type="italic">a gatherer of sycamore-fruit.</hi>" Our sycamores bear no fruit, but, it seems, theirs did, which Amos gathered either for his cattle or for himself and his family, or to sell. He was a plain country-man, bred up and employed in country work and used to country fare. He <hi type="italic">followed the flocks</hi> as well as the herds, and thence God <hi type="italic">took him,</hi> and bade him <hi type="italic">go</hi> and <hi type="italic">prophesy to his people Israel,</hi> deliver to them such messages as he should from time to time <hi type="italic">receive from the Lord.</hi> God made him a prophet, and a prophet to them, appointed him his work and appointed him his post. Therefore he ought not to be silenced, for, (1.) He could produce a divine commission for what he did. He did not run before he was sent, but pleads, as Paul, that he was <hi type="italic">called to be an apostle;</hi> and men will find it is at their peril if they contradict and oppose any that come in God's name, if they say to his <hi type="italic">seers, See not,</hi> or silence those whom he has bidden to speak; such <hi type="italic">fight against God.</hi> An affront done to an ambassador is an affront to the prince that sends him. Those that have a warrant from God ought not to <hi type="italic">fear the face of man.</hi> (2.) The mean character he wore before he received that commission strengthened his warrant, so far was it from weakening it. [1.] He had no thoughts at all of ever being a prophet, and therefore his prophesying could not be imputed to a raised expectation or a heated imagination, but purely to a divine impulse. [2.] He was not educated nor instructed in the art or mystery of prophesying, and therefore he must have his abilities for it immediately from God, which is an undeniable proof that he had his mission from him. The apostles, being originally unlearned and ignorant men, evidenced that they owed their knowledge to their having <hi type="italic">been with Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Acts iv. 13</reference>. When the treasure is put into such earthen vessels, it is thereby made to appear that the <hi type="italic">excellency of the power is of God, and not of man,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2 Cor. iv. 7</reference>. [3.] He had an honest calling, by which he could comfortably maintain himself and his family; and therefore did not need to prophesy for bread, as Amaziah suggested (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.12">v. 12</reference>), did not take it up as a trade to live by, but as a trust to honour God and do good with. [4.] He had all his days been accustomed to a plain homely way of living among poor husbandmen, and never affected either gaieties or dainties, and therefore would not have thrust himself so near the king's court and chapel if the business God had called him to had not called him thither. [5.] Having been so meanly bred, he could not have the courage to speak to kings and great men, especially to speak such bold and provoking things to them, if he had not been animated by a greater spirit than his own. If God, that sent him, had not strengthened him, he could not thus have <hi type="italic">set his face as a flint,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa. l. 7</reference>. Note, God often chooses the <hi type="italic">weak and foolish things of the world</hi> to confound the wise and mighty; and a herdman of Tekoa puts to shame a priest of Bethel, when he receives from God authority and ability to act for him. <div eID="gen20214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20215" type="x-p"/> 2. He condemns Amaziah for the opposition he gave them, and denounces the judgments of God against him, not from any private resentment or revenge, but in the name of the Lord and by authority from him, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.16-Amos.7.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Amaziah would not suffer Amos to preach at all, and therefore he is particularly ordered to preach against him: <hi type="italic">Now therefore hear thou the word of the Lord,</hi> hear it and tremble. Those that cannot bear general woes may expect woes of their own. The sin he is charged with is forbidding Amos to prophesy; we do not find that he beat him, or put him in the stocks, only he enjoined him silence: <hi type="italic">Prophesy not against Israel, and drop not thy word against the house of Isaac;</hi> he must not only thunder against them, but he must not so much as drop a word against them; he cannot bear, no, not the most gentle distilling of that rain, that small rain. Let him therefore hear his doom. <div eID="gen20215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20216" type="x-p"/> (1.) For the opposition he gave to Amos God will bring ruin upon himself and his family. This was the sin that filled the measure of his iniquity. [1.] He shall have no comfort in any of his relations, but be afflicted in those that were nearest to him: <hi type="italic">His wife shall be a harlot;</hi> either she shall be forcibly abused by the soldiers, as the Levite's concubine by the men of Gibeah (they <hi type="italic">ravish the women of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.5.11">Lam. v. 11</reference>), or she shall herself wickedly play the harlot, which, though her sin, her great sin, would be his affliction, his great affliction and reproach, and a just punishment upon him for promoting spiritual whoredom. Sometimes the sins of our relations are to be looked upon as judgments of God upon us. His children, though they keep honest, yet shall not keep alive: <hi type="italic">His sons and his daughters shall fall by the sword</hi> of war, and he himself shall live to see it. He has trained them up in iniquity, and therefore God will cut them off in it. [2.] He shall be stripped of all his estate; it shall fall into the hand of the enemy, and be <hi type="italic">divided by line,</hi> by lot, among the soldiers. What is ill begotten will not be long kept. [3.] He shall himself perish in a strange country, not in the <hi type="italic">land of Israel,</hi> which had been holiness to the Lord, but in a <hi type="italic">polluted land,</hi> in a heathen country, the fittest place for such a heathen to end his days in, that hated and silenced God's prophets and contributed so much to the polluting of his own land with idolatry. <div eID="gen20216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20217" type="x-p"/> (2.) Notwithstanding the opposition he gave to Amos, God will bring ruin upon the land and nation. He was accused for saying, <hi type="italic">Israel shall be led away captive</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.11">v. 11</reference>), but he stands to it, and repeats it; for the unbelief of man shall not make the word of God of no effect. The <hi type="italic">burden of the word of the Lord</hi> may be striven with, but it cannot be shaken off. Let Amaziah rage, and fret, and say what he will to the contrary, <hi type="italic">Israel shall surely go into captivity forth of his land.</hi> Note, it is to no purpose to contend with the judgments of God; for when God judges he will overcome. Stopping the mouths of God's ministers will not stop the progress of God's word, for it shall not return void.  <chapter eID="Amos.7"/> <div eID="gen20217" type="x-p"/>

entries.e09c04123b13e1aed9a46cbdc4d9169ac4c7755a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12604"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <div sID="gen23249" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Amos.7.1-Amos.7.9">Am. 7:1-9</reference>. The seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters contain Visions, with Their Explanations. The seventh chapter consists of two parts. First (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.1-Amos.7.9">Am 7:1-9</reference>): Prophecies Illustrated by Three Symbols: (1) A vision of grasshoppers or young locusts, which devour the grass, but are removed at Amos' entreaty; (2) Fire drying up even the deep, and withering part of the land, but removed at Amos' entreaty; (3) A plumb-line to mark the buildings for destruction. Secondly (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.10-Amos.7.17">Am 7:10-17</reference>): Narrative of Amaziah's Interruption of Amos in Consequence of the Foregoing Prophecies, and Prediction of His Doom.<div eID="gen23249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23250" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12604"/><hi type="bold">1. showed ... me; and, behold--</hi>The same formula prefaces the three visions in this chapter, and the fourth in <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1">Am 8:1</reference>.<div eID="gen23250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grasshoppers--</hi>rather, "locusts" in the caterpillar state, from a Hebrew root, "to creep forth." In the autumn the eggs are deposited in the earth; in the spring the young come forth [Maurer].<div eID="gen23251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the latter growth--</hi>namely, of grass, which comes up after the mowing. They do not in the East mow their grass and make hay of it, but cut it off the ground as they require it.<div eID="gen23252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king's mowings--</hi>the first-fruits of the mown grass, tyrannically exacted by the king from the people. The literal locusts, as in Joel, are probably symbols of human foes: thus the "growth" of grass "after the king's mowings" will mean the political revival of Israel under Jeroboam II (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>), after it had been mown down, as it were, by Hazael and Ben-hadad of Syria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.3">2Ki 13:3</reference>), [Grotius]. <div eID="gen23253" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc5ef0017f83674f060b5ec3bcf8a3341468a86d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12605"/><div sID="gen23254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12605"/><hi type="bold">2. by whom shall Jacob arise?--</hi>If Thou, O God, dost not spare, how can Jacob maintain his ground, reduced as he is by repeated attacks of the Assyrians, and erelong about to be invaded by the Assyrian Pul (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.20">20</reference>)? Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.19">Is 51:19</reference>. The mention of "Jacob" is a plea that God should "remember for them His covenant" with their forefather, the patriarch (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>).<div eID="gen23254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is small--</hi>reduced in numbers and in strength. <div eID="gen23255" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbc6323536b2b559dd7d8d5d686c57c8a5147f64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12606"/><div sID="gen23256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12606"/><hi type="bold">3. repented for this--</hi>that is, of this. The change was not in the mind of God (<reference osisRef="Num.2.19">Nu 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>), but in the effect outwardly. God unchangeably does what is just; it is just that He should hear intercessory prayer (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.16-Jas.5.18">Jas 5:16-18</reference>), as it would have been just for Him to have let judgment take its course at once on the guilty nation, but for the prayer of one or two righteous men in it (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.23-Gen.18.33">Ge 18:23-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.11">1Sa 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.42.10">Jr 42:10</reference>). The repentance of the sinner, and God's regard to His own attributes of mercy and covenanted love, also cause God outwardly to deal with him as if he repented (<reference osisRef="Jonah.3.10">Jon 3:10</reference>), whereas the change in outward dealing is in strictest harmony with God's own unchangeableness.<div eID="gen23256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">It shall not be--</hi>Israel's utter overthrow now. Pul was influenced by God to accept money and withdraw from Israel. <div eID="gen23257" type="x-p"/>
entries.a65ff89f39b31a29415c2751643e04bfd64b4bce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12607"/><div sID="gen23258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12607"/><hi type="bold">4. called to contend--</hi>that is, with Israel judicially (<reference osisRef="Job.9.3">Job 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Is 66:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.22">Eze 38:22</reference>). He ordered to come at His call the infliction of punishment by "fire" on Israel, that is, drought (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6-Amos.4.11">Am 4:6-11</reference>), [Maurer]. Rather, war (<reference osisRef="Num.21.28">Nu 21:28</reference>), namely, Tiglath-pileser [Grotius].<div eID="gen23258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devoured the ... deep--</hi>that is, a great part of Israel, whom he carried away. Waters are the symbol for many people (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Re 17:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">did eat up a part--</hi>namely, all the land (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">Am 4:7</reference>) of Israel east of Jordan (<reference osisRef="1Chr.5.26">1Ch 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Is 9:1</reference>). This was a worse judgment than the previous one: the locusts ate up the grass: the fire not only affects the surface of the ground, but burns up the very roots and reaches even to the deep. <div eID="gen23260" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c154f39c448c5ab9f2f81b78bd9e6652d439021: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12608"/><div sID="gen23261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12608"/><hi type="bold">7. wall made by a plumb-line--</hi>namely, perpendicular. <div eID="gen23261" type="x-p"/>
entries.638f91ed33a87baddb12f36fd14cee529ec51414: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12609"/><div sID="gen23262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12609"/><hi type="bold">8. plumb-line in ... midst of ... Israel--</hi>No longer are the symbols, as in the former two, stated generally; this one is expressly applied to Israel. God's long-suffering is worn out by Israel's perversity: so Amos ceases to intercede (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.33">Ge 18:33</reference>). The plummet line was used not only in building, but in destroying houses (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.13">2Ki 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Is 28:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">34:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">La 2:8</reference>). It denotes that God's judgments are measured out by the most exact rules of justice. Here it is placed "in the midst" of Israel, that is, the judgment is not to be confined to an outer part of Israel, as by Tiglath-pileser; it is to reach the very center. This was fulfilled when Shalmaneser, after a three years' siege of Samaria, took it and carried away Israel captive finally to Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3">2Ki 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.6">5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen23262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... pass by ... any more--</hi>not forgive them any more (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.2">Am 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.11">Pr 19:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>). <div eID="gen23263" type="x-p"/>
entries.0906b2f9d6f9bdf93f73a03dd96e922ad8f8ba81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12610"/><div sID="gen23264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12610"/><hi type="bold">9. high places--</hi>dedicated to idols.<div eID="gen23264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Isaac--</hi>They boasted of their following the example of their forefather Isaac, in erecting high places at Beer-sheba (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">Am 5:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.26.23">Ge 26:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.1">46:1</reference>); but he and Abraham erected them before the temple was appointed at Jerusalem--and to God; whereas they did so, after the temple had been fixed as the only place for sacrifices--and to idols. In the Hebrew here "Isaac" is written with s, instead of the usual ts; both forms mean "laughter"; the change of spelling perhaps expresses that their "high places of Isaac" may be well so called, but not as they meant by the name; for they are only fit to be laughed at in scorn. Probably, however, the mention of "Isaac" and "Israel" simply expresses that these names, which their degenerate posterity boasted in as if ensuring their safety, will not save them and their idolatrous "sanctuaries" on which they depended from ruin (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Am 8:14</reference>).<div eID="gen23265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of Jeroboam with ... sword--</hi>fulfilled in the extinction of Zachariah, son of Jeroboam II, the last of the descendants of Jeroboam I, who had originated the idolatry of the calves (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.8-2Kgs.15.10">2Ki 15:8-10</reference>).<div eID="gen23266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23267" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Amos.7.10-Amos.7.17">Am. 7:10-17</reference>. Amaziah's Charge against Amos: His Doom Foretold. <div eID="gen23267" type="x-p"/>
entries.c170941771da4d711487de9803231088b78e4c4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12611"/><div sID="gen23268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12611"/><hi type="bold">10. priest of Beth-el--</hi>chief priest of the royal sanctuary to the calves at Beth-el. These being a device of state policy to keep Israel separate from Judah. Amaziah construes Amos words against them as treason. So in the case of Elijah and Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17">1Ki 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.13">Jr 37:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.14">14</reference>). So the antitype Jesus was charged (<reference osisRef="John.19.12">Joh 19:12</reference>); political expediency being made in all ages the pretext for dishonoring God and persecuting His servants (<reference osisRef="John.11.48-John.11.50">Joh 11:48-50</reference>). So in the case of Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">Ac 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.5">24:5</reference>).<div eID="gen23268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst of ... Israel--</hi>probably alluding to Amos' own words, "in the midst of ... Israel" (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.8">Am 7:8</reference>), foretelling the state's overthrow to the very center. Not secretly, or in a corner, but openly, in the very center of the state, so as to upset the whole utterly.<div eID="gen23269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land is not able to bear all his words--</hi>They are so many and so intolerable. A sedition will be the result. The mention of his being "priest of Beth-el" implies that it was for his own priestly gain, not for the king or state, he was so keen. <div eID="gen23270" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d69442ae74ffbe10932b153c92cc45a6ac3c1d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12612"/><div sID="gen23271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12612"/><hi type="bold">11. Jeroboam shall die, &c.--</hi>Amos had not said this: but that "the house of Jeroboam" should fall "with the sword" (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.9">Am 7:9</reference>). But Amaziah exaggerates the charge, to excite Jeroboam against him. The king, however, did not give ear to Amaziah, probably from religious awe of the prophet of Jehovah. <div eID="gen23271" type="x-p"/>
entries.25067c596d5c5ccc7c7ffb4fac304eb592eac7ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12613"/><div sID="gen23272" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12613"/><hi type="bold">12. Also--</hi>Besides informing the king against Amos, lest that course should fail, as it did, Amaziah urges the troublesome prophet himself to go back to his own land Judah, pretending to advise him in friendliness.<div eID="gen23272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seer--</hi>said contemptuously in reference to Amos' visions which precede.<div eID="gen23273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there eat bread--</hi>You can earn a livelihood there, whereas remaining here you will be ruined. He judges of Amos by his own selfishness, as if regard to one's own safety and livelihood are the paramount considerations. So the false prophets (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.19">Eze 13:19</reference>) were ready to say whatever pleased their hearers, however false, for "handfuls of barley and pieces of bread." <div eID="gen23274" type="x-p"/>
entries.8722749748497c1b6264cb729ec15fbb549f9c5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12614"/><div sID="gen23275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12614"/><hi type="bold">13. prophesy not again--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.2.12">Am 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen23275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at Beth-el--</hi>Amaziah wants to be let alone at least in his own residence.<div eID="gen23276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king's chapel--</hi>Beth-el was preferred by the king to Dan, the other seat of the calf-worship, as being nearer Samaria, the capital, and as hallowed by Jacob of old (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.16">Ge 28:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.6">35:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">7</reference>). He argues by implication against Amos' presumption, as a private man, in speaking against the worship sanctioned by the king, and that in the very place consecrated to it for the king's own devotions.<div eID="gen23277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king's court--</hi>that is, residence: the seat of empire, where the king holds his court, and which thou oughtest to have reverenced. Samaria was the usual king's residence: but for the convenience of attending the calf-worship, a royal palace was at Beth-el also. <div eID="gen23278" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5b891aff60d4b31b17276c923be2add66cef9b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12615"/><div sID="gen23279" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12615"/><hi type="bold">14. I was no prophet--</hi>in answer to Amaziah's insinuation (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.12">Am 7:12</reference>), that he discharged the prophetical office to earn his "bread" (like Israel's mercenary prophets). So far from being rewarded, Jehovah's prophets had to expect imprisonment and even death as the result of their prophesying in Samaria or Israel: whereas the prophets of Baal were maintained at the king's expense (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.19">1Ki 18:19</reference>). I was not, says Amos, of the order of prophets, or educated in their schools, and deriving a livelihood from exercising the public functions of a prophet. I am a shepherd (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.7.15">Am 7:15</reference>, "flock"; the Hebrew for "herdsman" includes the meaning, shepherd, compare <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>) in humble position, who did not even think of prophesying among you, until a divine call impelled me to it.<div eID="gen23279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophet's son--</hi>that is, disciple. Schools of prophets are mentioned first in First Samuel; in these youths were educated to serve the theocracy as public instructors. Only in the kingdom of the ten tribes is the continuance of the schools of the prophets mentioned. They were missionary stations near the chief seats of superstition in Israel, and associations endowed with the Spirit of God; none were admitted but those to whom the Spirit had been previously imparted. Their spiritual fathers travelled about to visit the training schools, and cared for the members and even their widows (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1">2Ki 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>). The pupils had their common board in them, and after leaving them still continued members. The offerings which in Judah were given by the pious to the Levites, in Israel went to the schools of the prophets (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42">2Ki 4:42</reference>). Prophecy (for example, Elijah and Elisha) in Israel was more connected with extraordinary events than in Judah, inasmuch as, in the absence of the legal hierarchy of the latter, it needed to have more palpable divine sanction.<div eID="gen23280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sycamore--</hi>abounding in Palestine. The fruit was like the fig, but inferior; according to Pliny, a sort of compound, as the name expresses, of the fig and the mulberry. It was only eaten by the poorest (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">1Ki 10:27</reference>).<div eID="gen23281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gatherer--</hi>one occupied with their cultivation [Maurer]. To cultivate it, an incision was made in the fruit when of a certain size, and on the fourth day afterwards it ripened [Pliny, Natural History, 13.7,14]. Grotius from Jerome says, if it be not plucked off and "gathered" (which favors English Version), it is spoiled by gnats. <div eID="gen23282" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d8ecd9cff979efbf33b304f3d68f2d526c47f1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12616"/><div sID="gen23283" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12616"/><hi type="bold">15. took me as I followed the flock--</hi>So David was taken (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.8">2Sa 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.70">Psa 78:70</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.71">71</reference>). Messiah is the antitypical Shepherd (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6">Psa 23:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.1-John.10.18">Joh 10:1-18</reference>).<div eID="gen23283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto my people--</hi>"against" [Maurer]; so <reference osisRef="Amos.7.16">Am 7:16</reference>. Jehovah claims them still as His by right, though slighting His authority. God would recover them to His service by the prophet's ministry. <div eID="gen23284" type="x-p"/>
entries.60c0712c1aa0d9def0a9bd743ae271f5eb5bdd1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12617"/><div sID="gen23285" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12617"/><hi type="bold">16. drop--</hi>distil as the refreshing drops of rain (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.2">Eze 21:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Mic.2.6">Mi 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen23285" type="x-p"/>
entries.e82ca7cbad91461986265d71a8d989724b8aa20d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12618"/><div sID="gen23286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12618"/><hi type="bold">17. Thy wife shall be an harlot in the city--</hi>that is, shall be forced by the enemy, while thou art looking on, unable to prevent her dishonor (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.16">Is 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.11">La 5:11</reference>). The words, "saith THE Lord are in striking opposition to "Thou sayest" (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.16">Am 7:16</reference>).<div eID="gen23286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divided by line--</hi>among the foe.<div eID="gen23287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a polluted land--</hi>Israel regarded every foreign land as that which really her own land was now, "polluted" (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.5">Is 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.7">Jr 2:7</reference>). <chapter eID="Amos.7"/>

entries.e91e54ec44672fd4586ff1e41d80b8f11ec592e2: <div eID="gen34420" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34421" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34422" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34422" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34421" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34423" type="x-p"/> In this chapter God represents to Amos, by three several visions, the judgments he is about to bring on Israel. The first is a plague of locusts, threatening to cut of the hopes of the harvest by attacking it in the time of the second growth; the first luxuriances of the crop being probably mowed for the king's horses, <reference osisRef="Amo.7.1-Amo.7.3">Amo 7:1-3</reference>. The next vision threatens a judgment by fire, which would consume a great part, <reference osisRef="Amo.7.4-Amo.7.6">Amo 7:4-6</reference>; and the third a total overthrow of Israel, levelling it as it were by a line, <reference osisRef="Amo.7.7-Amo.7.9">Amo 7:7-9</reference>. The rest of the chapter is a denunciation of heavy judgments against Amaziah, priest of Beth-el, who had brought an accusation to the king against the prophet, <reference osisRef="Amo.7.10-Amo.7.17">Amo 7:10-17</reference>. <div eID="gen34423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34424" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34425" type="x-p"/> Behold, he formed grasshoppers - גבי gobai is generally understood here to signify locusts. See the notes on Joel 1 (note) and Joel 2 (note). <div eID="gen34425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34426" type="x-p"/> The shooting up of the latter growth - The early crop of grass had been already mowed and housed. The second crop or rowing, as it is called in some places, was not yet begun. By the king's mowings we may understand the first crop, a portion of which the king probably claimed as being the better hay; but the words may signify simply the prime crop, that which is the best of the whole. Houbigant thinks the shearing of the king's sheep is meant.
entries.b5b12c32ff65a5498662053aa2c686ab719ae7b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34427" type="x-p"/> By whom shall Jacob arise? - The locusts, the symbols of the many enemies that had impoverished Jerusalem, having devoured much of the produce of the land, were proceeding, till, at the intercession of the prophet, they were removed. Then, seeing in the light of prophecy the nation in every sense brought low, he cries, "By whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small." Calmet justly remarks: "After the death of Jeroboam the second, the kingdom, so flourishing and powerful before, was reduced to such weakness that it was obliged to have recourse to strangers for support. Menahem applied to Pul, king of Assyria, whence arose the final misery of the state.
entries.cb002bcbf5b447f9ae21e22370431e1cb452a8fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34428" type="x-p"/> The Lord repented - Changed his purpose of destroying them by the locusts. See <reference osisRef="Amo.7.6">Amo 7:6</reference>.
entries.25f9345dfe547b96292c5b9c2f7ef3cb684b05e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34429" type="x-p"/> The Lord God called to contend by fire - Permitted war, both civil and foreign, to harass the land, after the death of Jeroboam the second. These wars would have totally destroyed it, had not the prophet interceded. <div eID="gen34429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34430" type="x-p"/> It devoured the great deep, and did eat up a part - We are here to understand the partially destructive wars which afterwards took place; for the Lord causes all these things to pass before the eyes of Amos in the vision of prophecy; and intimates that, at the intercession of his prophets, total ruin should be prevented.
entries.cc25b1801102dd43a1e5608334679d6f0e342baf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34431" type="x-p"/> With a plumbline in his hand - This appears to be intended as an emblem of strict justice, and intimated that God would now visit them according to their iniquities.
entries.4833e7b8f613b31a6387de64ed1c27ad2e8f1824: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34432" type="x-p"/> I will set a plumbline - I will visit them by justice without any mixture of mercy.
entries.b5e49a7365eedc943034845e96c1b9d5ec3bdea0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34433" type="x-p"/> And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate - Their total destruction is at hand. The high place of Isaac was Beer-sheba, where Isaac had built an altar to the Lord, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.25">Gen 26:25</reference>. This high place, which had been abused to idolatrous uses, was demolished by Josiah, king of Judah, as we read in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.8">2Kgs 23:8</reference>, for he defiled all the high places from Geba to Beersheba. <div eID="gen34433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34434" type="x-p"/> I will rise against the house of Jeroboam - The Lord had promised to Jehu, the ancestor of Jeroboam, that his family should sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. Zechariah, the son of Jeroboam, was the fourth in order after Jehu; and on him the threatening in this verse fell; for he was murdered by Shallum after he had reigned six months, and in him the family became extinct. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.30">2Kgs 10:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.8-2Kgs.15.10">2Kgs 15:8-10</reference>.
entries.d51303cc33a6df603076703ec89460d97c15e4e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34435" type="x-p"/> Amaziah the priest of Beth-el - The idolatrous priest who had been established by the king to maintain the worship of the golden calves which Jeroboam the elder had set up at this place. <div eID="gen34435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34436" type="x-p"/> Amos hath conspired against thee - This was truly a lying prophet; there is not one word of truth in this message which he sent to Jeroboam. Amos had not conspired against the king - had not said that Jeroboam should die by the sword - and had not said that Israel should be carried away captive, though this last was implied in God's threatening and afterwards delivered by this prophet; see <reference osisRef="Amo.7.17">Amo 7:17</reference>.
entries.084e0b76adcc1c6aedb8dc4f2be0212be37c9505: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34437" type="x-p"/> O thou seer - He pretends kindness to the prophet, and counsels him to go into Judea, and prophesy there and be safe, even in the time that he had accused him of high treason against Jeroboam. Hireling priests of this kind have ever been the great enemies of the true prophets of God; and when they could bring no charge of false doctrine or immorality against them, have accused them of conspiring against the government; and because they have preached against sin, have held them up as exciting insurrection among the people.
entries.b2b7f085e6e1b0714a35dd73d95b906e3900e626: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34438" type="x-p"/> But prophesy not - at Beth-el - He must not speak against idolatry, because that was the king's religion; and he who speaks against the king's religion must be an enemy to the state. This was the doctrine held in England by popish James 2 and his insidious Jesuit hireling priests, till God in his mercy put this pitiful tyrant down, and with him his false prophets, and the degrading superstition which they endeavored to establish in these lands.
entries.e316bce0d79fc7528d64a022c606056a47502c67: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34439" type="x-p"/> I was no prophet - I am an extraordinary messenger of God. I am not called to the prophetic office but for this occasion. I have no message to Judah, and therefore need not go there. I have a message to Israel alone, and I must faithfully deliver it. <div eID="gen34439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34440" type="x-p"/> For the account which Amos gives here of himself, see the introduction.
entries.6cdb76e6748b63cbd934fd098dd2688d092397ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen34440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34441" type="x-p"/> Now therefore hear thou the word of the Lord - While he was speaking in his own vindication, God seems to have inspired him with the awful prediction which he immediately delivers.
entries.8020862e45ab1c83876aa003dbfc6ffa2228d00d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen34441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34442" type="x-p"/> Thy wife shall be a harlot - As this was the word of the Lord, so it was fulfilled; but as we have no farther account of this idolatrous priest, so we cannot tell in what circumstances these threatenings were executed. <div eID="gen34442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34443" type="x-p"/> 1. His wife was to be a public prostitute; she was probably such already privately in the temple, as the wife of an idolatrous priest. <div eID="gen34443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34444" type="x-p"/> 2. His sons and daughters were to fall by the sword. <div eID="gen34444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34445" type="x-p"/> 3. Their inheritance was to be taken by strangers. <div eID="gen34445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34446" type="x-p"/> 4. And himself was to die a captive in a heathen land. <div eID="gen34446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34447" type="x-p"/> Israel shall surety go into captivity - He now declares fully what he had not declared before, though Amaziah had made it a subject of accusation. This particular was probably revealed at this instant, as well as those which concerned Amaziah and his family.  <chapter eID="Amos.7"/> <div eID="gen34447" type="x-p"/>

entries.64dedbb74faab591fcee255bc36e6820c96ab01a: <div eID="gen16406" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Visions of the Locusts, the Fire, and the Plumb-Line. The Prophet’s Experience at Bethel - Amos 7 <reference osisRef="Amos.7.1-Amos.7.3">Amo 7:1-3</reference></title> <div sID="gen16407" type="x-p"/> The first two visions. - <reference osisRef="Amos.7.1">Amo 7:1</reference>-3. The Locusts. - Amo 7:1. <hi type="italic">“Thus the Lord Jehovah showed me; and, behold, He formed locusts in the beginning of the springing up of the second crop; and, behold, it was a second crop after the king’s mowing.</hi> Amo 7:2. <hi type="italic">And it came to pass, when they had finished eating the vegetable of the land, I said, Lord Jehovah, forgive, I pray: how can Jacob stand? for he is small.</hi> Amo 7:3. <hi type="italic">Jehovah repented of this: It shall not take place, saith Jehovah.” </hi> The formula, “Thus the Lord Jehovah showed me,” is common to this and the three following visions (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.4">Amo 7:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.7">Amo 7:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1">Amo 8:1</reference>), with this trifling difference, that in the third (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.7">Amo 7:7</reference>) the subject (the Lord Jehovah) is omitted, and <hi type="italic">'Adōnâi</hi> (the Lord) is inserted instead, after <hi type="italic">vehinnēh</hi> (and behold). הראני denotes seeing with the eyes of the mind - a visionary seeing. These visions are not merely pictures of a judgment which was ever threatening, and drawing nearer and nearer (Baur); still less are they merely poetical fictions, or forms of drapery selected arbitrarily, for the purpose of clothing the prophet’s thoughts; but they are inward intuitions, produced by the Spirit of God, which set forth the punitive judgments of God. <hi type="italic">Kōh</hi> (<hi type="italic">ita</hi>, thus) points to what follows, and <hi type="italic">vehinnēh</hi> (and behold) introduces the thing seen. Amos sees the Lord form locusts. Baur proposes to alter יוצר (forming) into יצר (forms), but without any reason, and without observing that in all three visions of this chapter <hi type="italic">hinnēh</hi> is followed by a participle (קרא in <reference osisRef="Amos.7.4">Amo 7:4</reference>, and נצּב in <reference osisRef="Amos.7.7">Amo 7:7</reference>), and that the <hi type="italic">'Adōnâi</hi> which stands before נצּב in <reference osisRef="Amos.7.7">Amo 7:7</reference> shows very clearly that this noun is simply omitted in <reference osisRef="Amos.7.1">Amo 7:1</reference>, because <hi type="italic">'AdōnâI Yehōvâh</hi> has immediately preceded it. גּבי (a poetical form for גּבה, analogous to שׂדי for שׂדה, and contracted into גּוב in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Nah 3:17</reference>) signifies locusts, the only question being, whether this meaning is derived from גּוּב = Arab. <hi type="italic">jâb</hi>, to cut, or from גּבה = Arab. <hi type="italic">jb‛a</hi>, to creep forth (out of the earth). The fixing of the time has an important bearing upon the meaning of the vision: viz., “at the beginning of the springing up of the second crop (of grass);” especially when taken in connection with the explanation, “after the mowings of the king.” These definitions cannot be merely intended as outward chronological data. For, in the first place, nothing is known of the existence of any right or prerogative on the part of the kings of Israel, to have the early crop in the meadow land throughout the country mown for the support of their horses and mules (1Ki 18:5), so that their subjects could only get the second crop for their own cattle. Moreover, if the second crop, “after the king’s mowings,” were to be interpreted literally in this manner, it would decidedly weaken the significance of the vision. For if the locusts did not appear till after the king had got in the hay for the supply of his own mews, and so only devoured the second crop of grass as it grew, this plague would fall upon the people alone, and not at all upon the king. But such an exemption of the king from the judgment is evidently at variance with the meaning of this and the following visions. Consequently the definition of the time must be interpreted spiritually, in accordance with the idea of the vision. The king, who has had the early grass mown, is Jehovah; and the mowing of the grass denotes the judgments which Jehovah has already executed upon Israel. The growing of the second crop is a figurative representation of the prosperity which flourished again after those judgments; in actual fact, therefore, it denotes the time when the dawn had risen again for Israel (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">Amo 4:13</reference>). Then the locusts came and devoured all the vegetables of the earth. עשׂב הארץ is not the second crop; for עשׂב does not mean grass, but vegetables, the plants of the field (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.1.11">Gen 1:11</reference>). <reference osisRef="Amos.7.2">Amo 7:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.7.3">Amo 7:3</reference> require that this meaning should be retained. When the locusts had already eaten the vegetables of the earth, the prophet interceded, and the Lord interposed with deliverance. This intercession would have been too late after the consumption of the second crop. On the other hand, when the vegetables had been consumed, there was still reason to fear that the consumption of the second crop of grass would follow; and this is averted at the prophet’s intercession. והיה for ויהי, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.48">1Sa 17:48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.11">Jer 37:11</reference>, etc. סלח־נא, pray forgive, sc. the guilt of the people (cf. Num 14:19). מי יקוּם, how (מי <hi type="italic">qualis</hi>) can Jacob (the nation of Israel) stand (not arise), since it is small? קטן, small, i.e., so poor in sources and means of help, that it cannot endure this stroke; not “so crushed already, that a very light calamity would destroy it” (Rosenmüller). for נחם על, see Exo 32:14. זאת (this) refers to the destruction of the people indicated in מי יקוּם; and זאת is also to be supplied as the subject to לא תהיה.
entries.ecda2b9b748a51036a2f4faf3842057bfe4db48f: <reference osisRef="Amos.7.4-Amos.7.6">Amo 7:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen16407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16408" type="x-p"/> The Devouring Fire. - Amo 7:4. <hi type="italic">“Thus the Lord Jehovah showed me: and, behold, the Lord Jehovah called to punish with fire; and it devoured the great flood, and devoured the portion.</hi> Amo 7:5. <hi type="italic">And I said, Lord Jehovah, leave off, I pray: how can Jacob stand? for it is small.</hi> Amo 7:6. <hi type="italic">Jehovah repented of this; this also shall not take place, said the Lord Jehovah.” </hi> That the all-devouring fire represents a much severer judgment than that depicted under the figure of the locusts, is generally acknowledged, and needs no proof. But the more precise meaning of this judgment is open to dispute, and depends upon the explanation of the fourth verse. The object to קרא is לריב בּאשׁ, and ריב is to be taken as an infinitive, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.13">Isa 3:13</reference> : He called to strive (i.e., to judge or punish) with fire. There is no necessity to supply <hi type="italic">ministros suos</hi> here. The expression is a concise one, for “He called to the fire to punish with fire” (for the expression and the fact, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Isa 66:16</reference>). This fire devoured the great flood. <hi type="italic">Tehōm rabbâh</hi> is used in <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen 7:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.51.10">Isa 51:10</reference>, etc., to denote the unfathomable ocean; and in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen 1:2</reference> <hi type="italic">tehōm</hi> is the term applied to the immense flood which surrounded and covered the globe at the beginning of the creation. ואכלה, as distinguished from ותּאכל, signifies an action in progress, or still incomplete (Hitzig). The meaning therefore is, “it also devoured (began to devour) <hi type="italic">'eth</hi>-<hi type="italic">hachēleq</hi>;” i.e., not the field, for a field does not form at all a fitting antithesis to the ocean; and still less “the land,” for <hi type="italic">chēleq</hi> never bears this meaning; but the inheritance or portion, namely, that of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">Deu 32:9</reference>), i.e., Israel. Consequently <hi type="italic">tehōm rabbâh</hi> cannot, of course, signify the ocean as such.
